new.title: Climb to Peyrepertuse, the castle in the clouds
new.desc: Perched on a ridge about 800 m high in the Corbières, Peyrepertuse is the largest of the Cathar castles. It was first mentioned in the 11th century and the upper keep of Saint-Jordi was added in 1242 after the crown took the fortress.
new.tip: Allow two to three hours including the steep path from the car park; the site closes in storms and strong wind. Wear sturdy shoes.

new.title: Stand on the last Cathar stronghold at Quéribus
new.desc: Quéribus, above Cucugnan, was the last Cathar bastion to fall to the crusaders, in 1255. It then served as a border fortress between France and Aragon until the Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659.
new.tip: Go early or late to avoid summer crowds and wind; the view reaches the Mediterranean and the Pyrenees. Combine with Peyrepertuse in one day.

new.title: Explore Puilaurens castle above the Boulzane valley
new.desc: Puilaurens is a well-preserved frontier fortress, ordered built by Guillaume de Peyrepertuse in 1229 and strengthened by Louis IX in 1255. It guarded the Aragon border until the Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659. It is one of the five Sons of Carcassonne.
new.tip: The walk up from the car park takes about 20 minutes; the castle is a good stop on the road to Axat and the Fenouillèdes.

new.title: See the ruins of Termes, the castle that held out in 1210
new.desc: Termes was held by Raymond de Termes and besieged by Simon de Montfort in 1210 in one of the hardest sieges of the Albigensian Crusade. The ruined castle stands in the wild Hautes-Corbières.
new.tip: Open in season with a small museum on site; the surrounding Termenès is best seen on a drive that also takes in Villerouge-Termenès.

new.title: Walk up to the four castles of Lastours
new.desc: Cabaret, Tour Régine, Surdespine and Quertinheux crown a rocky ridge about 300 m high above the Orbiel gorges. Pierre-Roger de Cabaret held Cabaret against Simon de Montfort in 1210 and surrendered in 1211.
new.tip: Start from the belvedere and the Maison du Patrimoine in Lastours village; the climb takes about 45 minutes. Wear good shoes.

new.title: Climb the great keep of Château d'Arques
new.desc: Gilles de Voisins began this Gothic castle around 1280, with a square keep 24 to 25 m high flanked by four corner turrets. The lordship came to his grandfather Pierre de Voisins, a lieutenant of Simon de Montfort. In 1575 only the keep resisted a Protestant siege.
new.tip: The village below is also pleasant; allow about an hour for the visit.

new.title: Discover Puivert castle and its troubadour musicians
new.desc: The castle at Puivert is known for the carved musicians in its keep, whose lute, psaltery, rebec and bagpipe are echoed in the nearby Musée du Quercorb. It sits in the Quercorb above a lake.
new.tip: Visit the Musée du Quercorb in the village for the reconstructed instruments and headphone troubadour songs.

new.title: Meet Bélibaste, the last Cathar, at Villerouge-Termenès
new.desc: Guilhem Bélibaste, the last known Occitan Cathar Perfect, was burned alive here in 1321. The castle of the archbishops of Narbonne now has an audiovisual tour contrasting his life with that of Archbishop Bernard de Farges.
new.tip: The castle also houses a medieval-style restaurant; combine with the Termes ruins nearby.

new.title: Tour the medieval abbey of Lagrasse
new.desc: Sainte-Marie d'Orbieu abbey, founded in the 8th century and confirmed by a Charlemagne diploma of 779, became one of the most powerful in southern France. The public part is owned by the Aude département and a community of canons regular has lived there since 2004.
new.tip: Allow nearly two hours for the full visit; the public rate was 7.50 euros adult at last report.

new.title: Wander the cloister and rose garden of Fontfroide
new.desc: This Cistercian abbey near Narbonne is known for its 12th to 13th century cloister and a terraced rose garden with around 2,000 to 2,500 rose bushes. The abbey site also has a wine cellar and restaurant.
new.tip: Allow one and a quarter to one and a half hours; free parking at the entrance. Roses peak in May and June.

new.title: Walk the Roman Horreum galleries under Narbonne
new.desc: These underground galleries date from the 1st century BC and lie about 5 m below the town centre, probably the foundations of a warehouse or market. They were discovered in 1838, listed in 1961 and opened to the public in 1976.
new.tip: Entrance is on rue Rouget-de-Lisle; part of the Narbo Via ticket group. It is cool and dry, good in rain.
new.q: Horreum romain, rue Rouget de Lisle, Narbonne

new.title: Admire the unfinished Gothic choir of Narbonne cathedral
new.desc: The cathedral of Saint-Just-et-Saint-Pasteur is limited to a grandiose choir because the Hundred Years' War stopped the project. The cloister linking it to the archbishops' palace was begun in 1349 and finished in 1417.
new.tip: Visit together with the archbishops' palace next door; check ticketing at the tourist office.
new.q: Cathédrale Saint-Just-et-Saint-Pasteur, Rue Armand Gautier, Narbonne

new.title: Climb the Gilles Aycelin keep of the archbishops' palace
new.desc: Built between 1295 and 1306 at the corner of the Palais Neuf, the square tower of Archbishop Gilles Aycelin is about 40 to 42 m high. The Palais des Archevêques also houses the city's art and history museum.
new.tip: The climb rewards you with views over the roofs of Narbonne; check opening hours before going.
new.q: Palais des Archevêques, Place de l'Hôtel de Ville, Narbonne

new.title: Discover Roman Narbonne at the Narbo Via museum
new.desc: The Foster + Partners museum opened in 2021 to display Narbonne's Roman heritage. Its lapidary wall holds about 800 funerary monument fragments and the entrance hall has a milestone naming Cnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, dated 122 to 118 BC.
new.tip: Allow two hours; combined tickets cover the Horreum and the Amphoralis site.
new.q: Narbo Via, 50 Avenue de Gruissan, Narbonne

new.title: Unravel the Saunière mystery at Rennes-le-Château
new.desc: The hilltop village is tied to the legend of the abbé Saunière, who began restoring the Sainte-Marie-Madeleine church in 1891. The Domaine includes the presbytery museum, Villa Béthanie, gardens and Tour Magdala, and the church holds a devil holding the holy-water stoup.
new.tip: Check seasonal hours; the Domaine ticket is separate from the church.

new.title: Drive the Pierre-Lys defile in the Gorges de l'Aude
new.desc: South of Quillan the Aude cuts through the Pierre-Lys gorge, with cliffs up to 700 m and the tunnel known as Trou du Curé. The Belvédère du Diable gives a view of the so-called devil's walls above the river.
new.tip: The D117 is a balcony road; stop at the viewpoints and watch for rafting groups on the river.

new.title: Visit the ruined abbey-cathedral of Alet-les-Bains
new.desc: Alet was a Benedictine abbey first mentioned in the 9th century and later a cathedral. Wars of Religion damage left the 12th-century Notre-Dame remains, chapter house and north gate. The village has about 21 listed monuments.
new.tip: Entry is arranged through the village tourist office; wander the half-timbered streets and the medieval bridge too.

new.title: See the Romanesque chevet of Caunes-Minervois abbey
new.desc: The Benedictine abbey of Caunes is known for one of the finest Romanesque apses in Languedoc. The village is also famous for its red marble, which came from quarries nearby.
new.tip: The abbey visit is paid; the village has a market on Fridays and the quarry walk starts nearby.

new.title: Explore Saissac castle in the Montagne Noire
new.desc: The Cathar-era castle of Saissac stands above the village on the southern edge of the Montagne Noire and has been listed since 1926. Museums in the village cover old trades, books and contemporary art, and a working paper mill survives in the forest.
new.tip: Combine with Cabrespine and the Lastours castles in a Montagne Noire loop.

new.title: Look into the Gouffre Géant de Cabrespine
new.desc: This giant chasm in the Montagne Noire is visited on balconies about 200 m above the bottom, with a classic guided tour of around 50 minutes. A guided visit of the underground river is offered on reservation.
new.tip: The visit involves stairs and narrow passages and is not wheelchair accessible; book the river tour ahead.
new.q: Gouffre Géant de Cabrespine, La Cresto, Cabrespine

new.title: Visit the Riquet obelisk at the Seuil de Naurouze
new.desc: The Seuil de Naurouze, at about 190 m above sea level, is the summit of the Canal du Midi. A 20 m obelisk built between 1825 and 1827 honours Pierre-Paul Riquet near the site of the old octagonal basin.
new.tip: Pleasant canalside stop for a picnic; reach it by bike from Castelnaudary in about an hour.
new.q: Obélisque de Riquet, Seuil de Naurouze, Montferrand

new.title: Stroll the Somail canal hamlet and its giant bookshop
new.desc: Le Somail is a stop on the Canal du Midi with an 18th-century bridge (Pont Saint-Marcel, 1773). Le Trouve Tout du Livre, an antiquarian bookshop in a former canalside storehouse at 28 allée de la Glacière, holds some 50,000 to 60,000 books.
new.tip: Check bookshop hours, which vary by season, and bring something to read on the towpath.
new.q: Le Trouve Tout du Livre, 28 Allée de la Glacière, Le Somail, Saint-Nazaire-d'Aude

new.title: Climb to the Tour Barberousse above Gruissan's circular village
new.desc: Old Gruissan is a circulade, a circular village wrapped around the ruined Barberousse tower on a rocky spur about 35 m high. The tower looks out over the lagoons and salt marshes; dates range from the 10th to the 13th century in different sources.
new.tip: Walk up through the streets at sunset; the village has many places to eat.

new.title: Drive through the Réserve Africaine de Sigean
new.desc: This drive-through safari park near Sigean is open every day of the year and also has a walking section. Full adult admission was from 34 euros in 2026.
new.tip: Book online; wind sometimes affects the visit, and the cut-off for the car safari is earlier than the walk-through park.

new.title: Hike up to the ruined castle of Aguilar
new.desc: Château d'Aguilar overlooks the Tuchan plain from a hill and has been listed since 1949. Olivier de Termes lost it in 1215; it was sold to Louis IX around 1262 and kept a border role until 1659. Two hexagonal rings of walls and half-round towers remain.
new.tip: Entry is free; a path of about 3 km links Tuchan to the castle on the Cathar GR trail.

new.title: Visit Saint-Hilaire, birthplace of Blanquette de Limoux
new.desc: Benedictine monks of the abbey of Saint-Hilaire are credited with the earliest recorded sparkling wine, Blanquette de Limoux, in 1531. The abbey keeps the sarcophagus of Saint Sernin, attributed to the Master of Cabestany. The claim that Dom Pérignon learnt the method here is doubtful.
new.tip: Pair with a Blanquette tasting at Limoux, a short drive away.

new.title: Eat grilled meat at Chez Bébelle in Les Halles
new.desc: Chez Bébelle is a grill counter inside the Narbonne market hall, known for brochettes, beef or horse tartare, entrecôte and grilled boudin. Its Sunday format has been a seafood and charcuterie brunch with regional wines.
new.tip: Go at lunchtime; the market is open 7 am to 2 pm. Glasses of wine were around 2.50 euros in the 2026 guide entry.
new.q: Chez Bébelle, Les Halles, Boulevard Docteur Ferroul, Narbonne

new.title: Try the town's cassoulet at the Maison du Cassoulet
new.desc: This bistro-style restaurant sits in the historic centre of Castelnaudary, the self-declared world capital of cassoulet, a short walk from the Canal du Midi.
new.tip: Cassoulet is a heavy dish; share a starter and walk by the Grand Bassin afterwards.

new.title: Taste cassoulet at the Maison Escudier workshop
new.desc: Maison Escudier, a charcuterie operating since 1920, offers group visits with a workshop tour, a documentary film and a tasting. Its jars and vacuum-packed cassoulet can be bought to take home.
new.tip: Reserve ahead for the organised tasting; the shop address is on rue de Dunkerque in some listings.
new.q: Maison Escudier, rue de Dunkerque, Castelnaudary

new.title: Eat lagoon eel at Le Portanel in Bages
new.desc: Le Portanel occupies a former fishermen's house on the Étang de Bages. Chef Jean-Christophe Rousseau calls the eel the star of his menu, and the fish of the day comes from the lagoon and market.
new.tip: Check closing days and payment options, as sources disagree. Menus ran about 21 to 42 euros before drinks.

new.title: Eat Gruissan oysters at La Cambuse du Saunier
new.desc: A restaurant on the salt marsh serving the oysters raised in the basins of the island with local dishes and wines. The oysters are described as iodised and subtly sweet.
new.tip: Located on Route de l'Ayrolle; book in summer.
new.q: La Cambuse du Saunier, Route de l'Ayrolle, Gruissan

new.title: Slurp oysters at Chez Cul d'Oursin in Leucate
new.desc: A family-run oyster bar in the Grau de Leucate port, founded in 2011, praised for its oysters and house white wine. Leucate's lagoon oysters are served in the local producers' huts.
new.tip: Hours vary by season; local huts sell a plate of oysters, mussels and clams for roughly 6 to 15 euros.
new.q: Chez Cul d'Oursin, Centre ostréicole, Mas n°40 Rive Droite, Port Leucate, Leucate

new.title: Lunch at La Table de Fontfroide in the old sheepfold
new.desc: The abbey restaurant occupies the abbey's former bergerie and serves Mediterranean cooking that includes vegetables from the abbey gardens. Bottles are Corbières from the Fontfroide terroir.
new.tip: Open for lunch from February to mid-December and for dinner in July and August; check ahead.
new.q: La Table de Fontfroide, Abbaye de Fontfroide, Narbonne

new.title: Taste seasonal cooking at Le Bastion, Lagrasse
new.desc: Le Bastion on the Promenade is a modern restaurant with a Michelin Plate. Chefs Fabien De Bruyn and Valentin Renaud cook creative dishes from local and seasonal produce.
new.tip: Book ahead for dinner; check the 2026 season dates.
new.q: Le Bastion, 50 boulevard de la Promenade, Lagrasse

new.title: Dine at Lionel Giraud's La Table Saint-Crescent
new.desc: Chef Lionel Giraud's restaurant in Narbonne is rated 17/20 by Gault&Millau as a Table de Prestige and is listed by the Michelin Guide. The cuisine is creative and personal.
new.tip: Budget about 120 to 220 euros per person; book well ahead.
new.q: Maison Saint-Crescent La Table Lionel Giraud, 68 avenue du Général Leclerc, Narbonne

new.title: Eat bistronomy at Le Petit Comptoir, Narbonne
new.desc: Le Petit Comptoir is a restaurant and wine bar on Boulevard Maréchal Joffre that dates from 1976 and holds a Michelin Plate. It serves refined bistro classics.
new.tip: Closed on Sundays; book for dinner.
new.q: Le Petit Comptoir, 4 Boulevard Maréchal Joffre, Narbonne

new.title: Order cassoulet at Le Grand Café on Limoux's square
new.desc: Le Grand Café on Place de la République is described as an institution serving traditional regional food including cassoulet and grills, with a terrace under the arcades.
new.tip: It is a good stop during Limoux's carnival weekends; the menu has a Café de Paris formula.
new.q: Le Grand Café, 25 place de la République, Limoux

new.title: Taste Occitan-Breton cooking at L'Odalisque, Limoux
new.desc: Chef Sven Choplin blends Occitan cooking with Breton roots at L'Odalisque, and a local review site recommends it as a place to taste Blanquette.
new.tip: Pair a dish with a glass of Blanquette de Limoux; book at weekends.

new.title: Dine on Corbières wines at Hostellerie des Corbières
new.desc: In Lagrasse, chef Julien Oracz serves traditional cooking revisited with a view over the Corbières landscape, with a wine list of local AOC and IGP Corbières.
new.tip: Check opening days, as the hostellerie is seasonal.

new.title: Eat at the medieval rotisserie in Villerouge's castle
new.desc: One wing of the castle of Villerouge-Termenès houses a medieval-style rotisserie restaurant, set in the building where the last Cathar perfect was burned in 1321.
new.tip: Combine with the castle's audiovisual visit; check seasonal opening and book in summer.

new.title: Browse the deli and world kitchen at Moksi Café, Lagrasse
new.desc: Moksi Café sits on the Place de la Halle with a world-cuisine and vegetarian focus and a delicatessen of quality produce.
new.tip: Lagrasse's Saturday market runs under the same halle.
new.q: Moksi Café, Place de la Halle, Lagrasse

new.title: Dine at ME. in the Grand Hôtel Moderne et Pigeon, Limoux
new.desc: ME. is the restaurant of the Grand Hôtel Moderne et Pigeon at 1 place du Général-Leclerc in Limoux, a former monastery dating from the early 16th century. It is listed in the Michelin Guide for modern cooking, with a patio and a 17th-century stained-glass window.
new.tip: Lunch runs Wednesday to Friday and dinner is mostly Friday; book ahead.
new.q: ME., Grand Hôtel Moderne et Pigeon, 1 place du Général-Leclerc, Limoux

new.title: Hike the Gorges de Galamus from Cubières-sur-Cinoble
new.desc: The Galamus gorge straddles the Aude and Pyrénées-Orientales; a loop of about 8.7 km and 3 hours takes in the gorge. Cave hermits settled here from the 7th century and the Ermitage Saint-Antoine is cut into the cliff.
new.tip: The trail is steep and the gravel slippery; wear good shoes. The D7 road through the gorge is narrow.

new.title: Go rafting in the Pierre-Lys gorge on the Aude
new.desc: A sporty rafting descent of about 7 km on the Aude starts from Belvianes-et-Cavirac near Axat and takes about 1h15 on the water. The gorge is also used for canyoning, climbing and hiking.
new.tip: Book with a local operator; the season depends on water levels.

new.title: Cycle the Canal du Midi from Castelnaudary to Naurouze
new.desc: The towpath between Seuil de Naurouze and Castelnaudary is about 13 km and 50 minutes by bike, passing locks along the Canal des 2 Mers à vélo route. Bike rental is available at Port-Lauragais.
new.tip: Rent electric bikes at Port-Lauragais; the route is rated for experienced cyclists.

new.title: Glide down the Canal de la Robine in an electric boat
new.desc: Les Petits Bateaux du Canal rent licence-free electric boats from the Promenade des Barques in Narbonne, from about 20 euros, and boat trips pass under the Pont des Marchands.
new.tip: The Pont des Marchands may be closed to walkers; check the tourist office.

new.title: Tour the salt pans of the Île Saint-Martin, Gruissan
new.desc: A guided walk of about 1h15 and 2 km explains salt production, birds and the pink basins. The shop sells fleur de sel de Gruissan, flavoured salts and local oils and honeys. Oysters are raised in the same site.
new.tip: Hours vary by season; guided departures run several times a day in summer.
new.q: Le Salin de l'Île Saint-Martin, Gruissan

new.title: Taste Limoux sparkling wines at Sieur d'Arques
new.desc: The cooperative, which took the Sieur d'Arques name in 1990, handles about 60 percent of Limoux production and offers visits, a wine museum and a commented tasting. Its ancestral-method Blanquette is made only from mauzac.
new.tip: Phone ahead to confirm tasting fees and hours.
new.q: Sieur d'Arques, avenue du Languedoc, Limoux

new.title: Taste Blanquette at Maison Guinot's light-and-sound cellar
new.desc: Maison Guinot, the oldest Blanquette house in Limoux (1875), runs a roughly 45 minute guided cellar visit with projections, ending in a tasting of Blanquette and Crémant. A longer 1h30 initiation is also offered.
new.tip: Book in advance; listing prices start around 8 euros for the light-and-sound visit.
new.q: Maison Guinot, 3 Chemin de Ronde, Limoux

new.title: Join the Limoux carnival under the arcades
new.desc: The Limoux carnival runs every weekend from January to March, with bands called Fécos and Goudils parading under the arcades of Place de la République. It closes with the judging and burning of the Carnival effigy.
new.tip: Parades are free; outings are at 11am, 5pm and 10pm. Check exact dates on limoux.fr.

new.title: Browse the Baltard market hall of Narbonne
new.desc: Les Halles de Narbonne, in Baltard style and opened in 1901 near the Canal de la Robine, have nearly 70 traders and were named France's finest market in 2022 by regional press. They are open daily 7am to 2pm.
new.tip: Arrive in the morning, service is reduced on Mondays; entrance is free.
new.q: Les Halles de Narbonne, Boulevard Docteur Ferroul, Narbonne

new.title: Swim at the Plage des Chalets, Gruissan
new.desc: Famous for about 1,300 stilted wooden chalets and the film 37°2 le matin, the beach is shallow for many metres and good for families, with kilometres of fine sand. It has lifeguard posts and large free car parks; kitesurfing is banned here.
new.tip: Take care when swell is high; paddle and kayak rentals are nearby.

new.title: Walk the Sentier du Guetteur on the Cap Leucate cliffs
new.desc: The 2h30 return walk starts at the Leucate-Plage semaphore and follows a coastal path along the cliff edge with views to the Pyrenees on clear days. La Plagette cove lies at the foot of the cliffs.
new.tip: Keep away from the edge when the tramontane blows.

new.title: Hike the Pech de Bugarach, highest peak of the Corbières
new.desc: The Pech de Bugarach, 1,230 m, is climbed from the village of Bugarach on a loop of about 11.8 km with 828 m of ascent. Other starts include Col du Linas and La Bastide.
new.tip: A demanding route with smooth, sometimes slippery rock; check trail and parking conditions first.

new.title: Walk the Étang du Doul loop from Peyriac-de-Mer
new.desc: An easy loop of roughly 6 km starts in Peyriac-de-Mer, with a wooden boardwalk over the lagoon and a viewpoint on the Étang de Bages-Sigean, a haven for flamingos and other birds.
new.tip: Parking around the étang at Peyriac may be paid.

new.title: Hike La Clape to the chapel of Notre-Dame des Auzils
new.desc: Routes from Gruissan climb through the Clape massif to the chapel, passing the Allée des Naufragés with its cenotaphs, the Jardin des Ermites and the marine cemetery. Views extend over Gruissan.
new.tip: The massif closes in periods of fire risk; check locally before setting out.

new.title: Walk to the Carrière du Roy red marble quarry at Caunes
new.desc: The Carrière du Roy, worked by the Romans and made royal in 1692, supplied marble for Versailles, the Grand Trianon and the Louvre. It is no longer in operation and can be visited freely.
new.tip: Guided visits are run by Les Marbrières de Caunes; the working Terralbes quarry is seen only on guided safaris.

new.title: Spend a beach day at Narbonne-Plage
new.desc: The seaside station of Narbonne has about five kilometres of fine sand and a Blue Flag since 1988, with lifeguards in summer. The Créneau Naturel beach to the west looks towards Gruissan, and Karantes is near the marina.
new.tip: Supervised swimming runs only in summer; dogs are accepted at Créneau Naturel according to one listing.

new.title: Swim in the thermal outdoor pool at Alet-les-Bains
new.desc: Alet-les-Bains has springs described as the oldest mineral water in operation in France. The village's outdoor pool is filled with mineral water naturally heated to 24 degrees and is open only in summer.
new.tip: Hours are listed for about 19 June to 29 August; check before going.
new.q: Piscine d'eau minérale, Chemin des eaux chaudes, Alet-les-Bains

new.title: Soak at the Thermes de Rennes-les-Bains
new.desc: The spa at 30 Grande Rue des Thermes treats rheumatism and osteoarthritis and has an outdoor pool of warm thermal water at about 35 degrees. Springs range from about 37 to 46 degrees depending on the source.
new.tip: One directory says it is open April to November; confirm dates.
new.q: Thermes de Rennes-les-Bains, 30 Grande Rue des Thermes, Rennes-les-Bains

new.title: Shop the Saturday market under Lagrasse's medieval halle
new.desc: Lagrasse, a Plus Beaux Villages de France since 1986, keeps a Saturday market under its 14th-century halle. The Pont Vieux crosses the Orbieu to the abbey and has been dated to the 13th or 14th century.
new.tip: Go on Saturday morning, then cross the Pont Vieux to the abbey.
new.q: Halle de Lagrasse, Place de la Halle, Lagrasse
